> 艮。艮其背，不獲其身；行其庭，不見其人，無咎。

Hexagram 52 is about stopping, and the character's original sense is the opposite of stillness.

## 艮 is 很 — two eyes that will not give way

說文: 艮，很也。從匕目。匕目，猶目相匕，不相下也.

Original sense: stubborn — two gazes meeting, neither conceding, locked.

So 止 is not 艮's original sense. It comes from the卦象, two mountains standing side by side.

Between "not yielding" and "stopping" there is one extension.

Which matters, because readers of the 易 tend to take the hexagram's sense as the character's sense. There is no "quiet" in 艮. There is only "will not back off" — and a mountain sits on it.

## 背: the place you cannot see

背 is the back, behind the eyes.

So 艮其背 is stopping at the place that is not seen — not "looking inward at the spine."

Wang Bi's line reads it that way. The other line, which reads it as an internal-alchemical contemplation of the spine, is a much later usage. This book takes the old gloss.

Which is a much better image: the thing that is stopped is the thing behind you, the thing you cannot watch. Not the object of attention — the place attention does not reach.

## 趾、腓、限、身、輔

趾: the toes.
腓: the calf, the flesh behind the shin.
輔: the side-rail of a cart, borrowed for the jawbone.
身: the trunk.

And 限 needs care: built on 阜, its original sense is a barrier (說文 限，阻也). Commentators gloss it as the waist-hip boundary, taking the image from the body; the character's own sense is "the line."

So line three's problem is not the waist. It is the line that has been jammed.

## 列其夤

夤 is the flesh along the spine. 列 is 裂 — split.

The flesh of the back torn open.

The most painful sentence in the hexagram, and its point: when the stopping is done wrong, it hurts in the body. 厲薰心 — dangerous, and it smokes at the heart.

## 敦艮

Top line 敦艮，吉.

敦: thick.

Not "trying to stop." Thick enough that stopping is not needed — the kind of solidity that holds without being held.

## 上下敵應

敵: of equal force. 應: to respond.

敵應 — the corresponding lines are the same polarity, so they do not respond.

This is a description of the hexagram's body, not a moral judgement. It is not saying 艮 is cold; it is saying why 不見其人 is possible: nothing is pulled toward anything.

## The test

Take a thing you have been trying to hold still — a habit, a temper, a plan. Ask where you are stopping: at the toes, the calf, the waistline, the trunk, the jaw. Line three is the tell: if it hurts along the spine and smokes at the heart, the line has been jammed rather than drawn.
